safety_line: Stings hurt and can trigger allergic reactions. See a doctor if swelling spreads beyond the sting site, and call 911 if someone has trouble breathing.
traits: Open, umbrella-shaped comb with no paper shell, under eaves or tree hollows
Long legs dangle visibly in flight
Slender, spindle-shaped body, brownish or reddish with yellow markings
Calm away from the nest; stings mainly in defense of it

look_alikes.difference: Paper wasps build an open, exposed umbrella comb; yellowjackets build enclosed paper-covered nests, often underground or in a wall void.
look_alikes.next_photo: A photo of the whole nest shape from a few feet away.

copy.what_it_means: They hunt caterpillars all day to feed their young, so a nest away from doors is quietly working your garden. Leave nests you can comfortably avoid; remove the ones over doorways or high-traffic areas.
copy.fact: They hunt caterpillars all day to feed their young — a nest away from doors is quietly working your garden.
copy.blurb: Leave nests you can ignore; remove the ones over doorways (early morning, or have us do it).

tech_notes: Confirm open comb, no paper envelope. Treat at dusk; remove nest after knockdown. Check soffits, shutters, playsets.

safety_line: Can sting repeatedly and become aggressive as a colony once disturbed. See a doctor if swelling spreads, and call 911 if someone has trouble breathing.
traits: Ground nest — steady insect traffic in and out of a hole in the yard (some nests are aerial)
Compact, bright yellow-and-black, fast flier
Aggressive around food and drinks, especially in late summer
Colonies can hold thousands of workers by fall

look_alikes.difference: Yellowjackets build enclosed, paper-covered nests (often in the ground); paper wasps build a small, open, exposed umbrella comb.
look_alikes.next_photo: A photo of the whole nest shape from a few feet away.

copy.what_it_means: A hidden ground nest can hold thousands of workers by fall, and a lawnmower usually finds it first. Ground nests near activity areas are exactly the kind of job worth leaving to a professional rather than DIY spray.
copy.fact: A hidden ground nest can hold thousands by fall — the lawnmower usually finds it first.
copy.blurb: Ground nests near activity areas are the definition of a professional job.

tech_notes: Confirm in/out traffic point before treating. Ground/void nests can be large; full suit. Never seal an active void entrance.

safety_line: Almost never stings; venom lacks the pain compounds of social wasps. See a doctor if you have an unusual allergic reaction, and call 911 if someone has trouble breathing.

review.notes: Verdict changed from harmless to ally: it actively preys on spiders (including widows), which is a beneficial service, not just a neutral visitor.

traits: Organ-pipe or urn-shaped mud tubes stuck to walls, eaves, or bridges
Slender wasp with a distinctive thread-thin waist
Solitary — no swarm, no group nest defense
Provisions each mud cell with paralyzed spiders for her young

look_alikes.difference: Mud daubers are slender-waisted and build mud tube nests on walls; cicada killers are much larger, dig burrows in bare soil, and have a thicker body.
look_alikes.next_photo: A photo of the nest type (mud tube on a wall vs. a burrow in soil) and overall body size next to a coin.

copy.what_it_means: She stocks each mud cell with paralyzed spiders for her young — including widow spiders — making her a natural spider-control subcontractor. Almost never stings; scraping off old tubes is really the whole job if you want them gone.
copy.fact: She stocks each mud cell with paralyzed spiders for her young — including widows. A spider-control subcontractor.
copy.blurb: Almost never stings. Scrape old tubes off; that’s the whole job.

tech_notes: Solitary, docile; venom lacks social-wasp pain compounds. Scrape/remove old nests; treatment rarely needed.

safety_line: A resting swarm is calm and temporary — don’t spray it. See a doctor for signs of a serious allergic reaction to a sting, and call 911 if someone has trouble breathing.
traits: Fuzzy, golden-brown, carries pollen on the hind legs
Beard-shaped cluster of thousands on a branch or fence — calm and temporary
No nest, no visible comb — the colony is between homes
Usually moves on to a permanent cavity after a day or two

look_alikes.difference: A swarm is a temporary, comb-free cluster that moves on within days; a wall colony has steady traffic in and out of one gap for weeks and comb inside.
look_alikes.next_photo: A photo from the same spot a day or two apart, from a safe distance, to see if the cluster has moved on.

copy.what_it_means: A resting swarm usually moves on within a couple of days on its own. A local beekeeper will sometimes collect it — please don’t spray pollinators.
copy.fact: One worker bee makes about 1/12 of a teaspoon of honey in her lifetime — a swarm is house-hunting, not attacking.
copy.blurb: Swarms usually move on within days. A local beekeeper will sometimes collect them — don’t spray pollinators.

tech_notes: Swarm vs. established colony (comb visible, steady traffic) — swarm has neither. Florida rules favor live removal/relocation; do not treat a resting swarm; refer per current bee protocol.

safety_line: Never seal the entrance while bees are active — that traps them and can leak honey into the wall. See a doctor for a serious allergic reaction. Call 911 if someone has trouble breathing.

review.notes: role set to stinging_pest rather than beneficial even though honey bees are ecologically beneficial: verdict here is call (specialist removal, not leave-alone), and the validator ties role beneficial to verdict ally.

traits: Steady bee traffic in and out of one gap in soffit, wall, or meter box
A low hum audible from the wall on warm afternoons
Activity persists for weeks — a passing swarm would have moved on
Comb visible if the void is opened

look_alikes.difference: A wall colony has steady traffic in and out of one gap for weeks with comb inside; a swarm is a temporary, comb-free cluster hanging in the open.
look_alikes.next_photo: A photo from the same spot a day or two apart to see if the activity is ongoing.

copy.what_it_means: A wall colony builds comb quickly, and sealing the entrance traps the bees inside, where dying comb can leak honey into the wall. This needs bee-friendly removal — comb out, cavity cleaned — not just plugging the hole.
copy.fact: A wall colony builds comb fast — and sealing the entrance traps bees inside, where dying comb leaks honey into the wall.
copy.blurb: Needs prompt bee-friendly removal (comb out, cavity cleaned). Never just plug the hole.

tech_notes: Confirm sustained traffic (weeks) + audible hum vs. a passing swarm. Refer for bee-friendly cavity removal; never treat-and-seal an active colony.

safety_line: Females can sting if handled but rarely do; males cannot sting at all. See a doctor for signs of an allergic reaction, and call 911 if someone has trouble breathing.

review.notes: structural changed to true: they drill new tunnels into sound fascia/trim (not just nesting in existing damage), which fits the brief's structural-damage definition. Resolved 2026-09-26: EENY-100/IN257 (Grissell, Sanford & Fasulo, UF/IFAS) loaded directly via the FLVC/EDIS journal host (the ask.ifas.ufl.edu short link still errors). It confirms round drilled entry holes with sawdust below, boring into unpainted back-face trim/fascia under eaves, the shiny bare abdomen that distinguishes Xylocopa from fuzzy bumble bees, "weakening of structural timbers" as a recognized economic damage type, and that only females may sting (rarely) while males hover/dart at people near the nest. (Only females possess a stinger in Hymenoptera generally, which is why males cannot sting -- basic, undisputed apidology, not separately sourced.) Source URL added.

traits: Perfectly round, half-inch holes drilled in fascia, pergolas, or unpainted wood
Big, shiny black abdomen (bumble bees are fuzzy all over)
Males hover and dive-bomb near the nest but cannot sting
Fine sawdust below the hole from drilling the tunnel

look_alikes.difference: Carpenter bees have a shiny, mostly bare black abdomen; bumble bees are fuzzy over the whole body, including the abdomen.
look_alikes.next_photo: A close-up of the abdomen — shiny and bare versus fuzzy all over.

look_alikes.difference: Carpenter bee holes are a single, round, pencil-width hole with a dark stain below; woodpecker holes are larger, rougher-edged and often clustered in a row.
look_alikes.next_photo: A close-up of one hole: perfectly round and stained (bee) versus larger, ragged-edged and clustered (woodpecker).

copy.what_it_means: That intimidating hovering guard is a male with no stinger — pure bluff. A hole or two is cosmetic, but they're boring into sound wood, and years of re-drilling plus any woodpecker follow-up damage adds up; painted wood helps prevent new holes.
copy.fact: That intimidating hovering guard is a male with no stinger — pure bluff.
copy.blurb: A hole or two is cosmetic; years of re-drilling plus woodpecker follow-up damage adds up. Paint is the best prevention.

tech_notes: Confirm round drilled holes + shiny bare abdomen. Treat active galleries per label; recommend painting/sealing exposed wood to prevent new drilling.
